claim: Action Potential (APs) patterns of sensory cortex neurons encode a variety of stimulus features.
source: Action Potential (APs) patterns of sensory cortex neurons encode a variety of stimulus features, but how can a neuron change the feature to which it responds?
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory cortex function that draws from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: In vivo, a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) protocol consisting of pairing a postsynaptic AP with visually driven presynaptic inputs modifies a neurons' AP-response in a bidirectional way that depends on the relative AP-timing during pairing.
source: Here, we show that in vivo a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) protocol—consisting of pairing a postsynaptic AP with visually driven presynaptic inputs—modifies a neurons' AP-response in a bidirectional way that depends on the relative AP-timing during pairing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Postsynaptic APs repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses.
source: Whereas postsynaptic APs repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses, APs repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce AP responses to visual stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: APs repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce AP responses to visual stimulation.
source: Whereas postsynaptic APs repeatedly following presynaptic activation can convert subthreshold into suprathreshold responses, APs repeatedly preceding presynaptic activation reduce AP responses to visual stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Changes in AP responses were paralleled by restructuring of the neurons response to surround stimulus locations.
source: These changes were paralleled by restructuring of the neurons response to surround stimulus locations and membrane-potential time-course.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Changes in AP responses were paralleled by restructuring of the membrane-potential time-course.
source: These changes were paralleled by restructuring of the neurons response to surround stimulus locations and membrane-potential time-course.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Computational simulations could reproduce the observed subthreshold voltage changes only when presynaptic temporal jitter was included.
source: Computational simulations could reproduce the observed subthreshold voltage changes only when presynaptic temporal jitter was included.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: STDP rules can modify output patterns of sensory neurons.
source: Together this shows that STDP rules can modify output patterns of sensory neurons and the timing of single-APs plays a crucial role in sensory coding and plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The timing of single-APs plays a crucial role in sensory coding and plasticity.
source: Together this shows that STDP rules can modify output patterns of sensory neurons and the timing of single-APs plays a crucial role in sensory coding and plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The formation of sensory percepts in the mammalian cortex is thought to involve the propagation of action potentials through populations of connected neurons in response to sensory stimulation.
source: The formation of sensory percepts in the mammalian cortex is thought to involve the propagation of action potentials through populations of connected neurons in response to sensory stimulation (Hebb, 1949; Harris, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rules that dictate changes in the strength, or efficacy, of connections rely on persistent correlated activity between the connected neurons.
source: Rules that dictate changes in the strength, or efficacy, of these connections rely on persistent correlated activity between the connected neurons (for recent review, see Abraham, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: For changes in synaptic efficacy to be functional and recognized by the down-stream neurons targeted by the axon, the changes need to influence AP patterns.
source: For these changes in synaptic efficacy to be functional and recognized by the down-stream neurons targeted by the axon, the changes need to influence AP patterns.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional requirements of synaptic plasticity.

claim: Plasticity induction involving precisely timed action-potentials is known as spike-timing-dependent plasticity.
source: Plasticity induction involving precisely timed action-potentials, known as spike-timing-dependent plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998), has been suggested as a candidate mechanism to determine which stimulus driven inputs are strengthened and weakened (out of the many possible sensory driven inputs).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to foundational STDP papers.

claim: STDP has been suggested as a candidate mechanism to determine which stimulus driven inputs are strengthened and weakened.
source: Plasticity induction involving precisely timed action-potentials, known as spike-timing-dependent plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998), has been suggested as a candidate mechanism to determine which stimulus driven inputs are strengthened and weakened (out of the many possible sensory driven inputs).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the properties of STDP.

claim: The low numbers of APs and low repetition frequencies used to induce plastic changes in STDP protocols are consistent with low AP firing rates observed in awake freely moving animals exploring a novel environment.
source: What makes STDP rules so appealing for modification of synaptic strength in the cortex is that the low numbers of APs and low repetition frequencies used to induce plastic changes in STDP protocols (Feldman, 2012) are consistent with low AP firing rates observed in awake freely moving animals exploring a novel environment (Lee et al., 2006; Sawinski et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cortical neurons are capable of AP-responses that are temporally precise over multiple trials.
source: In addition, cortical neurons are capable of AP-responses that are temporally precise over multiple trials (Bair and Koch, 1996; Marsalek et al., 1997; Tchumatchenko et al., 2011), similar to the precision typically used during STDP pairing protocols (for recent review see, Feldman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Most modeling studies of synaptic plasticity using STDP rules assume that synaptic modification leads to changes in spiking.
source: Lastly, most modeling studies of synaptic plasticity using STDP rules assume that synaptic modification leads to changes in spiking (Gerstner et al., 1996; Song and Abbott, 2001) with a recent study suggesting that STDP underlies sensory map plasticity in the young and adult cortex (Young et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: A recent study suggests that STDP underlies sensory map plasticity in the young and adult cortex.
source: Lastly, most modeling studies of synaptic plasticity using STDP rules assume that synaptic modification leads to changes in spiking (Gerstner et al., 1996; Song and Abbott, 2001) with a recent study suggesting that STDP underlies sensory map plasticity in the young and adult cortex (Young et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Evidence for single-neuron STDP in vivo remains scarce and confined to subthreshold changes.
source: However, evidence for single-neuron STDP in vivo remains scarce and confined to subthreshold changes (Meliza and Dan, 2006; Jacob et al., 2007) and remains controversial (Lisman and Spruston, 2005, 2010; Fregnac et al., 2010; Shouval et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evidence for single-neuron STDP in vivo remains controversial.
source: However, evidence for single-neuron STDP in vivo remains scarce and confined to subthreshold changes (Meliza and Dan, 2006; Jacob et al., 2007) and remains controversial (Lisman and Spruston, 2005, 2010; Fregnac et al., 2010; Shouval et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies expressing controversy.

claim: Extracellular studies have suggested STDP can modify spiking patterns in anesthetized animals.
source: While extracellular studies have suggested STDP can modify spiking patterns in anesthetized (Fu et al., 2002) and freely moving animals (Celikel et al., 2004), this evidence remains difficult to interpret without information on single-cell membrane potential dynamics.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Extracellular studies have suggested STDP can modify spiking patterns in freely moving animals.
source: While extracellular studies have suggested STDP can modify spiking patterns in anesthetized (Fu et al., 2002) and freely moving animals (Celikel et al., 2004), this evidence remains difficult to interpret without information on single-cell membrane potential dynamics.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Evidence from extracellular studies remains difficult to interpret without information on single-cell membrane potential dynamics.
source: While extracellular studies have suggested STDP can modify spiking patterns in anesthetized (Fu et al., 2002) and freely moving animals (Celikel et al., 2004), this evidence remains difficult to interpret without information on single-cell membrane potential dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of extracellular recording methods.

claim: Visual cortex neuronal responses and receptive fields are known to be highly plastic.
source: The visual cortex is perfectly suited to study STDP since visual cortex neuronal responses and receptive fields are known to be highly plastic (Gilbert, 1998), and sensory maps can undergo plastic changes with experience (Daw and Wyatt, 1976; Li et al., 2008) or after removal of visual input (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963; Kaas et al., 1990; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sensory maps can undergo plastic changes with experience.
source: The visual cortex is perfectly suited to study STDP since visual cortex neuronal responses and receptive fields are known to be highly plastic (Gilbert, 1998), and sensory maps can undergo plastic changes with experience (Daw and Wyatt, 1976; Li et al., 2008) or after removal of visual input (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963; Kaas et al., 1990; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sensory maps can undergo plastic changes after removal of visual input.
source: The visual cortex is perfectly suited to study STDP since visual cortex neuronal responses and receptive fields are known to be highly plastic (Gilbert, 1998), and sensory maps can undergo plastic changes with experience (Daw and Wyatt, 1976; Li et al., 2008) or after removal of visual input (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963; Kaas et al., 1990; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During visual stimulation, the action potential output for many visual cortex neurons is tuned to specific locations in the visual field and to specific stimulus features.
source: Finally during visual stimulation, the action potential output for many visual cortex neurons is tuned to specific locations in the visual field and to specific stimulus features (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), even though each neuron receives synaptic inputs corresponding to surrounding locations or many different stimulus features (Ferster, 1986; Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a classic study.

claim: Each visual cortex neuron receives synaptic inputs corresponding to surrounding locations or many different stimulus features.
source: Finally during visual stimulation, the action potential output for many visual cortex neurons is tuned to specific locations in the visual field and to specific stimulus features (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), even though each neuron receives synaptic inputs corresponding to surrounding locations or many different stimulus features (Ferster, 1986; Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All ongoing membrane potential voltage fluctuations and spiking at the cell soma were measured and taken into account when presenting the stimulus.
source: We used STDP protocols similar to those previously applied in vivo (Meliza and Dan, 2006), but with the difference that all ongoing membrane potential voltage fluctuations and spiking at the cell soma were measured and taken into account when presenting the stimulus, since large membrane potential fluctuations (Cowan and Wilson, 1994) can alter a neuron's spiking responses (Petersen et al., 2003; Sachdev et al., 2004) and ongoing spiking may influence plasticity outcome (Sjostrom et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study.

claim: Large membrane potential fluctuations can alter a neuron's spiking responses.
source: We used STDP protocols similar to those previously applied in vivo (Meliza and Dan, 2006), but with the difference that all ongoing membrane potential voltage fluctuations and spiking at the cell soma were measured and taken into account when presenting the stimulus, since large membrane potential fluctuations (Cowan and Wilson, 1994) can alter a neuron's spiking responses (Petersen et al., 2003; Sachdev et al., 2004) and ongoing spiking may influence plasticity outcome (Sjostrom et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing spiking may influence plasticity outcome.
source: We used STDP protocols similar to those previously applied in vivo (Meliza and Dan, 2006), but with the difference that all ongoing membrane potential voltage fluctuations and spiking at the cell soma were measured and taken into account when presenting the stimulus, since large membrane potential fluctuations (Cowan and Wilson, 1994) can alter a neuron's spiking responses (Petersen et al., 2003; Sachdev et al., 2004) and ongoing spiking may influence plasticity outcome (Sjostrom et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Whole-cell recordings were targeted to Layer 2/3 neurons in the binocular primary visual cortex using intrinsic imaging followed by two-photon microscopy.
source: We targeted whole-cell recordings (Margrie et al., 2003) to Layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons in the binocular primary visual cortex (n = 58 rats) using intrinsic imaging followed by two-photon microscopy as using stereotaxic coordinates alone can be inaccurate (Slotnick and Brown, 1980; Kline and Reid, 1984).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Using stereotaxic coordinates alone can be inaccurate for targeting visual cortex.
source: We targeted whole-cell recordings (Margrie et al., 2003) to Layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons in the binocular primary visual cortex (n = 58 rats) using intrinsic imaging followed by two-photon microscopy as using stereotaxic coordinates alone can be inaccurate (Slotnick and Brown, 1980; Kline and Reid, 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All neurons were identified as L2/3 pyramidal neurons, based on firing pattern, location below the pia and morphology after post hoc histological staining.
source: All neurons (n = 71, yielding 72 data points, see 'Materials and methods') were identified as L2/3 pyramidal neurons, based on firing pattern, location below the pia and morphology after post hoc histological staining.
evidence: This describes the cell type identification methodology.

claim: A bar was flashed (500 ms) every 3–4 s at one of four non-overlapping spatial positions for visual stimulation.
source: For visual stimulation, a bar was flashed (500 ms) (Figure 1A) every 3–4 s at one of four non-overlapping spatial positions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the visual stimulation protocol and references Figure 1.

claim: Stimuli were always presented after the membrane potential had transitioned from an up-state into a down-state.
source: To measure ongoing spiking and membrane potential fluctuations, and to reduce variance and maximize consistency in the evoked responses (Petersen et al., 2003; Sachdev et al., 2004), we recorded in current clamp mode and always presented stimuli after the membrane potential had transitioned from an up-state into a down-state (Figure 1C), during which far fewer spontaneous synaptic inputs occur (Waters and Helmchen 2006).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and references Figure 1C.

claim: During down-states far fewer spontaneous synaptic inputs occur.
source: To measure ongoing spiking and membrane potential fluctuations, and to reduce variance and maximize consistency in the evoked responses (Petersen et al., 2003; Sachdev et al., 2004), we recorded in current clamp mode and always presented stimuli after the membrane potential had transitioned from an up-state into a down-state (Figure 1C), during which far fewer spontaneous synaptic inputs occur (Waters and Helmchen 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All four stimulus positions evoked either subthreshold or suprathreshold responses.
source: All four stimulus positions evoked either subthreshold or suprathreshold responses, consistent with the broad receptive fields of neurons in younger rats (Fagiolini et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Neurons in younger rats have broad receptive fields.
source: All four stimulus positions evoked either subthreshold or suprathreshold responses, consistent with the broad receptive fields of neurons in younger rats (Fagiolini et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mean subthreshold responses reached an initial peak 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, then decayed to a trough within 100–200 ms.
source: Mean subthreshold responses reached an initial peak 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, then decayed to a trough within 100–200 ms (Figure 1D), though considerable variability (Hirsch et al., 2002) was observed in the peak time, response shape, and amplitude across neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Considerable variability was observed in the peak time, response shape, and amplitude across neurons.
source: Mean subthreshold responses reached an initial peak 50–150 ms after stimulus onset, then decayed to a trough within 100–200 ms (Figure 1D), though considerable variability (Hirsch et al., 2002) was observed in the peak time, response shape, and amplitude across neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 1D and a citation.

claim: After a stable baseline period (9.0 ± 1.3 min, 32.4 ± 1.9 presentations of each stimulus, n = 32 recordings), an STDP induction protocol was applied by pairing single-APs with visual stimulation at only one of the four stimulus positions.
source: After a stable baseline period (9.0 ± 1.3 min, 32.4 ± 1.9 presentations of each stimulus, n = 32 recordings), we applied an STDP induction protocol by pairing single-APs, evoked by brief depolarizing current pulses, with visual stimulation at only one of the four stimulus positions (42.0 ± 1.5 pairing trials, 1.3 ± 0.16 APs/trial, n = 32, Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with specific quantitative details.

claim: The timing of the pairing spikes was individually chosen for each neuron to occur either before ('negative timing inductions', n = 17) or after the initial peak ('positive timing inductions', n = 15).
source: Since each neuron's response time was different, the timing of the pairing spikes was individually chosen for each neuron to occur either before ('negative timing inductions', n = 17, example in Figure 1E, left) or after the initial peak ('positive timing inductions', n = 15, example in Figure 1E, right).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The time of pairing spikes ranged from 82 ms before the response peak to 62 ms after.
source: As a result, by taking all recordings together based on whether the pairing spike was delivered before (red, negative timing) or after (green, positive timing) the initial peak, the time of pairing spikes ranged from 82 ms before the response peak to 62 ms after (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Responses at the paired position were changed, with the direction of the change strongly dependent on whether the pairing spike appeared before or after the response peak.
source: Responses at the paired position were changed, with the direction of the change strongly dependent on the whether the pairing spike appeared before or after the response peak (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Figure 2B,C.

claim: In neurons that received negative timing inductions the peak voltage amplitude significantly decreased by 26.4 ± 4.6% (n = 17) or 3.5 ± 0.7 mV (p<0.0001).
source: As expected (for review see, Bi and Poo, 2001) in neurons that received negative timing inductions the peak voltage amplitude significantly decreased by 26.4 ± 4.6% (n = 17) or 3.5 ± 0.7 mV (Figure 2C, p<0.0001), while positive timing inductions increased the peak voltage amplitude by 22.5 ± 8.7 % (n = 15) or 1.4 ± 0.6 mV (Figure 2C, p=0.025).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result with statistical significance.

claim: Positive timing inductions increased the peak voltage amplitude by 22.5 ± 8.7 % (n = 15) or 1.4 ± 0.6 mV (p=0.025).
source: As expected (for review see, Bi and Poo, 2001) in neurons that received negative timing inductions the peak voltage amplitude significantly decreased by 26.4 ± 4.6% (n = 17) or 3.5 ± 0.7 mV (Figure 2C, p<0.0001), while positive timing inductions increased the peak voltage amplitude by 22.5 ± 8.7 % (n = 15) or 1.4 ± 0.6 mV (Figure 2C, p=0.025).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result with statistical significance.

claim: The largest initial peak changes were not around t = 0 but were scattered from 0–50 ms on either side of t = 0.
source: The difference between what was observed here compared to previous in vitro (Bi and Poo, 2001) and in vivo studies (Fregnac et al., 2010) was that although the direction of the plasticity observed in responses to visual stimulation depended on spike timing, the largest initial peak changes were not around t = 0 but were scattered from 0–50 ms on either side of t = 0.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data that differs from previous studies.

claim: In most neurons that received positive timing inductions sensory-evoked spiking rates increased after the pairing protocol.
source: In most neurons that received positive timing inductions sensory-evoked spiking rates increased after the pairing protocol (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Of the 15 neurons tested with positive timing, 11 showed an increase in the average number of APs evoked by stimulus presentation, 1 showed a decrease, and 3 never discharged a stimulus-evoked AP.
source: Specifically, of the 15 neurons tested, 11 showed an increase in the average number of APs evoked by stimulus presentation, 1 showed a decrease, and 3 never discharged a stimulus-evoked AP (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In eight neurons the paired stimulus evoked spiking only after induction, that is over 50% transitioned from non-spiking to spiking.
source: Strikingly, in eight neurons the paired stimulus evoked spiking only after induction, that is over 50% transitioned from non-spiking to spiking.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result showing a major effect of the STDP protocol.

claim: Over the 15 neurons tested with positive timing, an additional 0.11 ± 0.06 APs per stimulus were observed for the paired stimulus position after induction (p=0.01, initial response 0.06 ± 0.04 APs per stimulus).
source: Over the 15 neurons tested, an additional 0.11 ± 0.06 APs per stimulus were observed for the paired stimulus position after induction (p=0.01, initial response 0.06 ± 0.04 APs per stimulus).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result with statistical significance.

claim: In four cases increases in AP firing were significant at the single-neuron level (p<0.05), despite the modest numbers of stimulus presentation trials and low firing rates.
source: In four cases increases in AP firing were significant at the single-neuron level (p<0.05), despite the modest numbers of stimulus presentation trials and low firing rates (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: For negative timing inductions, after pairing, the average number of APs evoked by stimulus presentation decreased (0.18 ± 0.10 APs per stimulus after induction, p=0.04, n = 15).
source: After pairing, the average number of APs evoked by stimulus presentation decreased (0.18 ± 0.10 APs per stimulus after induction, p=0.04, n = 15).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result with statistical significance.

claim: Of 15 neurons tested with negative timing, 12 showed a decrease in spiking and 3 an increase after induction.
source: Of these 15 neurons 12 showed a decrease in spiking and 3 an increase after induction (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: For negative timing, changes in spiking were statistically significant at the single-neuron level (p<0.05) in four cases, all of which showed a decrease in spiking.
source: These changes were statistically significant at the single-neuron level (p<0.05) in four cases, all of which showed a decrease in spiking.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Changes in spiking responses observed after STDP induction could not be accounted for by neurons becoming more depolarized (down-state membrane potential −64.8 ± 1.5 mV before vs −64.2± 1.5 mV after, p=0.61, n = 32).
source: These changes in spiking responses observed after STDP induction could not be accounted for by neurons becoming more depolarized (down-state membrane potential −64.8 ± 1.5 mV before vs −64.2± 1.5 mV after, p=0.61, n = 32) or by input resistance changes (323 ± 39 MΩ before vs 419 ± 54 MΩ after, p=0.16), and neither depolarization nor input resistance changes were correlated with changes in spiking (p>0.05).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that observed effects are not due to changes in baseline properties.

claim: Changes in spiking responses could not be accounted for by input resistance changes (323 ± 39 MΩ before vs 419 ± 54 MΩ after, p=0.16).
source: These changes in spiking responses observed after STDP induction could not be accounted for by neurons becoming more depolarized (down-state membrane potential −64.8 ± 1.5 mV before vs −64.2± 1.5 mV after, p=0.61, n = 32) or by input resistance changes (323 ± 39 MΩ before vs 419 ± 54 MΩ after, p=0.16), and neither depolarization nor input resistance changes were correlated with changes in spiking (p>0.05).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that observed effects are not due to changes in input resistance.

claim: In a control group, where visual stimuli were presented but no APs were paired, stimulus-driven spiking rates in the second half of the recording were not significantly different from the first half (p=0.20, four neurons with four positions each).
source: In a control group, where visual stimuli were presented but no APs were paired, stimulus-driven spiking rates in the second half of the recording were not significantly different from the first half (p=0.20, four neurons with four positions each), indicating that the increase in spiking was due to the STDP protocol.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating that the observed effects are due to the STDP protocol.

claim: Increases in AP firing at the paired position for positive timing inductions remained significant even after removing the two neurons exhibiting the greatest increases (p=0.036, n = 13).
source: Finally, we note that increases in AP firing at the paired position for positive timing inductions remained significant even after removing the two neurons exhibiting the greatest increases (p=0.036, n = 13).
evidence: This is a robustness check showing that the results are not driven by outliers.

claim: For positive timing experiments, stimulus positions immediately adjacent to the pairing position showed an increase of 0.10 ± 0.05 APs per stimulus (p=0.02, n = 15).
source: Compared to the average 0.11 ± 0.05 additional APs per stimulus evoked at the pairing position after induction, stimulus positions immediately adjacent to the pairing position also showed an increase nearly as large (0.10 ± 0.05 APs per stimulus, p=0.02, n = 15).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result showing spatial transfer of plasticity.

claim: The increase in AP firing diminished for more distant positions and was no longer significant for stimulus positions not immediately adjacent to the paired position (p>0.05).
source: This increase in AP firing diminished for more distant positions (Figure 3G) and was no longer significant for stimulus positions not immediately adjacent to the paired position (p>0.05).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the spatial extent of plasticity effects.

claim: In negative timing experiments, changes in AP firing were not significant at any non-paired positions (p>0.05).
source: In negative timing experiments, changes in AP firing were not significant at any non-paired positions (p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: After stimulus-AP pairing with positive timing, the stimulus response center moved toward the pairing position.
source: This analysis showed a simple but robust trend in the positive timing experiments: after stimulus-AP pairing, the stimulus response center moved toward the pairing position (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 3F.

claim: The shift in the suprathreshold response center was strongly correlated with the difference between pairing position and the response center before pairing (R = 0.81, p=0.008).
source: The shift in the suprathreshold response center was strongly correlated with the difference between pairing position and the response center before pairing (R = 0.81, p=0.008).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For negative timing inductions the majority of response centers moved away from the pairing position, but these changes were small and the trend was not significant (p=0.70).
source: For the negative timing inductions the majority of response centers moved away from the pairing position, but these changes were small and the trend was not significant (p=0.70).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Subthreshold response centers shifted toward the pairing position for positive timings (R = 0.53, p=0.04).
source: Subthreshold response centers, calculated by weighting each position by the peak amplitude, also shifted toward the pairing position for positive timings, albeit much less robustly than the suprathreshold shifts (R = 0.53, p=0.04, Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For negative timings subthreshold response centers tended to move away from the paired position, but these changes were too small to be significant (p>0.05).
source: As with the suprathreshold response centers, for negative timings subthreshold response centers tended to move away from the paired position, but these changes were too small to be significant (p>0.05, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: STDP protocols induce a rearrangement of the sub- and suprathreshold receptive field structure, especially for positive timing protocols.
source: These results show that STDP protocols induce a rearrangement of the sub- and suprathreshold receptive field structure, especially for positive timing protocols.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: STDP protocols in vivo can simultaneously induce potentiation and depression in the membrane potential of the same neuron.
source: This showed that STDP protocols in vivo can simultaneously induce potentiation and depression in the membrane potential of the same neuron (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The average membrane potential change was biphasic with an increase before the spike (maximum increase 0.84 mV at 64.5 ms before, p=0.04) and a decrease thereafter (maximum decrease 1.4 mV at 43.5 ms after, p=0.01).
source: Thus, in contrast to traditional STDP analysis where a neuron provides only a single data point on a graph of time difference vs response change (Figure 2C), both potentiation and depression occur for each neuron as a continuous function of time that on average is biphasic (Figure 5B, black line) with an increase before the spike (maximum increase 0.84 mV at 64.5 ms before, p=0.04) and a decrease thereafter (maximum decrease 1.4 mV at 43.5 ms after, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result with statistical significance shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Changes in membrane potential were strongest at the paired position, with similarly shaped but smaller changes at adjacent positions consistent with overlap in synaptic inputs, and nondescript changes at more distant positions.
source: Changes in membrane potential were strongest at the paired position, with similarly shaped but smaller changes at adjacent positions consistent with overlap in synaptic inputs, and nondescript changes at more distant positions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The shape of membrane potential changes was qualitatively similar to the biphasic STDP curve observed in vitro, but the positive and negative peaks were temporally further away from the pairing spike and shape of the curve were much broader in vivo.
source: While the shape of these membrane potential changes was qualitatively similar to the biphasic STDP curve observed in vitro (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998), the positive and negative peaks were temporally further away from the pairing spike and shape of the curve were much broader in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current in vivo results and previous in vitro studies.

claim: Introducing jitter into the presynaptic activity caused the positive and negative peaks of the change in membrane potential to broaden and become more distant from the pairing spike with increasing jitter.
source: However, introducing jitter into the presynaptic activity (Figure 5G) caused the positive and negative peaks of the change in membrane potential to broaden and become more distant from the pairing spike with increasing jitter (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 5G.

claim: With a presynaptic jitter of 40 ms the model produced a biphasic change in the mean membrane potential that closely resembled the in vivo experimental results, with a maximal potentiation 50 ms before and maximal depression 74 ms after the postsynaptic spike.
source: With a presynaptic jitter of 40 ms the model produced a biphasic change in the mean membrane potential (Figure 5H,I) that closely resembled the in vivo experimental results (Figure 5B), with a maximal potentiation 50 ms before and maximal depression 74 ms after the postsynaptic spike.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figures 5H,I.

claim: The model reproduced partial transfer of STDP effects to neighboring stimulus positions in a spike timing dependent manner given the assumption that a subset of presynaptic neurons respond with similar spiking patterns for multiple stimulus positions.
source: The model also reproduced partial transfer of STDP effects to neighboring stimulus positions (Figure 5J, red) in a spike timing dependent manner (Figure 5K) and given the assumption that a subset of presynaptic neurons respond with similar spiking patterns for multiple stimulus positions.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figures 5J,K.

claim: The membrane potential changes observed in vivo are broader than those observed in vitro and the broader time course can be explained by variably-timed inputs.
source: These modeling results show that the membrane potential changes observed in vivo are broader than those observed in vitro and that the broader time course can be explained by variably-timed inputs (but see Lin et al., 2003; Froemke et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2009 for alternative sources of broader STDP windows).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results with citations to alternative explanations.

claim: The slight transfer of changes in synaptic strength from one stimulus position to the next within a receptive field can be explained by partial overlap of the inputs activated by different stimuli.
source: Additionally, the slight transfer of changes in synaptic strength from one stimulus position to the next within a receptive field can be explained by partial overlap of the inputs activated by different stimuli as previously suggested (Meliza and Dan, 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results supported by a citation.

claim: An STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can convert a neuron's visually evoked responses from non-spiking to spiking.
source: Our results demonstrate that an STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can convert a neuron's visually evoked responses from non-spiking to spiking, can increase and diminish existing spiking responses, and can induce a rearrangement of the neurons sub- and suprathreshold responses to stimuli presented at locations surrounding the paired location.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: An STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can increase and diminish existing spiking responses.
source: Our results demonstrate that an STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can convert a neuron's visually evoked responses from non-spiking to spiking, can increase and diminish existing spiking responses, and can induce a rearrangement of the neurons sub- and suprathreshold responses to stimuli presented at locations surrounding the paired location.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: An STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can induce a rearrangement of the neurons sub- and suprathreshold responses to stimuli presented at locations surrounding the paired location.
source: Our results demonstrate that an STDP protocol using less than 50 paired APs can convert a neuron's visually evoked responses from non-spiking to spiking, can increase and diminish existing spiking responses, and can induce a rearrangement of the neurons sub- and suprathreshold responses to stimuli presented at locations surrounding the paired location.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: The current findings extend knowledge about STDP-induced subthreshold changes in vivo to the suprathreshold domain.
source: Our current findings extend our knowledge about STDP-induced subthreshold changes in vivo (Meliza and Dan, 2006; Jacob et al., 2007) to the suprathreshold domain.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings relative to previous work.

claim: The study provides a bridge between changes in spiking observed across many neurons' receptive fields after alteration of sensory input and subtle changes in subthreshold responses induced by STDP at the single neuron level.
source: Our study also provides a bridge between the changes in spiking observed across many neurons' receptives fields after alteration of sensory input for example through retinal lesions (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963; Kaas et al., 1990; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992) and subtle changes in subthreshold responses induced by STDP at the single neuron level both in vitro (Magee and Johnston, 1997; Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998) and in vivo (Meliza and Dan, 2006; Jacob et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings with citations to relevant previous work.

claim: A connection between receptive field plasticity, rearrangement of a neuron's tuning properties and STDP has been suggested by theoretical studies but has not been shown experimentally to date.
source: Such a connection between receptive field plasticity, rearrangement of a neuron's tuning properties and STDP has been suggested by theoretical studies (Song and Abbott, 2001; Young et al., 2007), but to date has not been shown experimentally.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical studies and notes the novelty of the current experimental findings.

claim: The rates of AP activity used in the pairing protocols were similar to activity reported for upper cortical layer populations in the visual cortex of both headfixed awake and freely exploring rodents.
source: As the rates of AP activity used in the pairing protocols was similar to activity reported for upper cortical layer populations in the visual cortex of both headfixed awake (Greenberg et al., 2008) and freely exploring rodents (Sawinski et al., 2009), this form of plasticity could represent a more general plasticity principle that relies on low firing rates and is central to individual neurons joining or leaving cell-assemblies, as proposed by Donald Hebb (Hebb, 1949).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This form of plasticity could represent a more general plasticity principle that relies on low firing rates and is central to individual neurons joining or leaving cell-assemblies.
source: As the rates of AP activity used in the pairing protocols was similar to activity reported for upper cortical layer populations in the visual cortex of both headfixed awake (Greenberg et al., 2008) and freely exploring rodents (Sawinski et al., 2009), this form of plasticity could represent a more general plasticity principle that relies on low firing rates and is central to individual neurons joining or leaving cell-assemblies, as proposed by Donald Hebb (Hebb, 1949).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Purely subthreshold manipulation of the postsynaptic voltage could have caused similar, or even stronger effects of Hebbian plasticity.
source: We cannot exclude, however, that purely subthreshold manipulation of the postsynaptic voltage could have caused similar, or even stronger effects of Hebbian plasticity (Lisman and Spruston, 2005, 2010; Fregnac et al., 2010; Shouval et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Hebbian synaptic plasticity also manifests itself in experimental protocols manipulating firing rates and postsynaptic voltage.
source: While STDP highlights the timing-dependence on a millisecond time scale, Hebbian synaptic plasticity also manifests itself in experimental protocols manipulating firing rates and postsynaptic voltage (Artola et al., 1990; Sjostrom et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous models assuming that Hebbian synaptic plasticity depends critically on postsynaptic voltage have allowed general theories of plasticity with both rate- and timing-dependent plasticity as special cases.
source: In fact, previous models assuming that Hebbian synaptic plasticity depends critically on postsynaptic voltage, have allowed general theories of plasticity with both rate- and timing-dependent plasticity as special cases (Clopath et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous modeling study.

claim: Optimality theories of STDP have proposed that the fundamental reason why pre-before-post induces LTP is to strengthen the causal link between input and output.
source: Optimality theories of STDP developed over the last 10 years, have proposed that the fundamental reason why pre-before-post induces LTP is to strengthen the causal link between input and output.
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical frameworks for understanding STDP.

claim: The optimal timing between pre- and post should be related to the rise time or width of the PSP caused by the presynaptic input.
source: Thus, the optimal timing between pre- and post should be related to the rise time or width of the PSP caused by the presynaptic input (Pfister et al., 2006; Bohte and Mozer, 2007; Toyoizumi et al., 2007; Parra et al., 2009; Hennequin et al., 2010; Pool and Mato, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: There is no similar optimality theory as to why synaptic depression should be spike-triggered.
source: There is no similar optimality theory as to why synaptic depression should be spike-triggered, as unspecific forms of depression of synapses (not temporally linked to the output spike) would work just as well from a theoretical point of view (Pfister et al., 2006; Bohte and Mozer, 2007; Toyoizumi et al., 2007; Hennequin et al., 2010; Pool and Mato, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Timing based post-before-pre LTD (negative timing) is a robust mechanism for manipulating neuronal spiking responses along with the previously proposed pre-before post LTP (positive timing).
source: What our study proposes is that timing based post-before-pre LTD (negative timing) is a robust mechanism for manipulating neuronal spiking responses along with the previously proposed pre-before post LTP (positive timing) (Gerstner et al., 1996; Song and Abbott, 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings with citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The study shows a robust timing effect for the change in voltage of the initial peak, where negative timing protocols produced decreased synaptic efficacy and positive timing protocols resulted in an increased synaptic efficacy, similar to that seen in vitro.
source: The present study shows a robust timing effect for the change in voltage of the initial peak, where negative timing protocols produced decreased synaptic efficacy and positive timing protocols resulted in an increased synaptic efficacy, similar to that seen in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings comparing them to in vitro results.

claim: The reported lack of dependence of the peak changes on the millisecond timescale is not consistent with previous in vitro STDP studies.
source: What is not consistent with previous in vitro STDP studies, where synaptic efficacy changes were derived from post-synaptic potentials, is our reported lack of dependence of the peak changes on the milisecond timescale.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and previous in vitro studies.

claim: From in vitro studies it would be expected that a pre- before post pairing with a delay during pairing of around 40 ms would produce almost no change and a pre- before post with a delay of around 2 ms would produce the most change.
source: From in vitro studies it would be expected that a pre- before post pairing with a delay during pairing of around 40 ms would produce almost no change and a pre- before post with a delay of around 2 ms would produce the most change (Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: This statement is based on a citation to a previous in vitro study.

claim: The discrepancy with previous studies is due to the complexity of in vivo responses to visual stimulation which are made up of an avalanche of both inhibitory and excitatory synaptic events.
source: We suggest that this discrepancy with previous studies (also see Fregnac et al., 2010) is due to the complexity of in vivo responses to visual stimulation which are made up of an avalanche of both inhibitory and excitatory synaptic events (Hirsch et al., 1998; Okun and Lampl, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to previous studies.

claim: The absolute voltage changes brought about by STDP were on the order of 2 mV, yet such a change was sufficient to significantly alter the stimulus evoked spiking probability.
source: The absolute voltage changes brought about by STDP in our study were on the order of 2 mV, yet such a change was sufficient to significantly alter the stimulus evoked spiking probability.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Small voltage changes have a dramatic effect on spiking output.
source: Hence, our study suggests that small voltage changes have a dramatic effect on spiking output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Complex membrane-potential waveforms at the soma in vitro can reliably generate spikes.
source: Despite these in vivo uncertainties, complex membrane-potential waveforms at the soma in vitro can reliably generate spikes (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995) and recent simulations paired with experiments (Tchumatchenko et al., 2011) show that cortical pyramidal neurons can rapidly and reliably change firing rates in response to very small changes in somatic depolarization and hyperpolarization (twofold spiking difference induced with a 40 pA current injection).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cortical pyramidal neurons can rapidly and reliably change firing rates in response to very small changes in somatic depolarization and hyperpolarization (twofold spiking difference induced with a 40 pA current injection).
source: Despite these in vivo uncertainties, complex membrane-potential waveforms at the soma in vitro can reliably generate spikes (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995) and recent simulations paired with experiments (Tchumatchenko et al., 2011) show that cortical pyramidal neurons can rapidly and reliably change firing rates in response to very small changes in somatic depolarization and hyperpolarization (twofold spiking difference induced with a 40 pA current injection).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules using very few pairing APs can turn a neuron that hitherto did not emit a spike in response to a visual stimulus into one that frequently spikes.
source: In the current study we show that spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules using very few pairing APs can turn a neuron that hitherto did not emit a spike in response to a visual stimulus into one that frequently spikes, while pairing APs with a different timing can reduce established spiking.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Pairing APs with a different timing can reduce established spiking.
source: In the current study we show that spike-timing-dependent plasticity rules using very few pairing APs can turn a neuron that hitherto did not emit a spike in response to a visual stimulus into one that frequently spikes, while pairing APs with a different timing can reduce established spiking.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: This is a fundamental mechanism by which neurons join and leave cell-assemblies.
source: We propose that this is a fundamental mechanism by which neurons join and leave cell-assemblies (Wallace and Kerr, 2010) as previously proposed (Hebb, 1949) in which very few precisely timed spikes select specific temporal synaptic sequences for long-term storage from the many that are activated during a sensory learning process.
evidence: This is a proposal about the broader significance of the findings with citations.

claim: Very few precisely timed spikes select specific temporal synaptic sequences for long-term storage from the many that are activated during a sensory learning process.
source: We propose that this is a fundamental mechanism by which neurons join and leave cell-assemblies (Wallace and Kerr, 2010) as previously proposed (Hebb, 1949) in which very few precisely timed spikes select specific temporal synaptic sequences for long-term storage from the many that are activated during a sensory learning process.
evidence: This is a proposal about the mechanism with citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Changes in tuning have direct implications for the function of neuronal circuits in which the respective neuron is embedded.
source: Since these spikes will be transmitted to hundreds of other downstream neurons, such a change in tuning has direct implications for the function of neuronal circuits in which the respective neuron is embedded.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Recorded neurons were located in primary visual cortex in L2/3, 169 ± 3 µm below the pial surface (range 112–225 μm, median = 170 μm).
source: Recorded neurons were located in primary visual cortex in L2/3, 169 ± 3 µm below the pial surface (range 112–225 μm, median = 170 μm; lower quartile = 150 μm; upper quartile = 186 μm) and within the responsive area identified with intrinsic optical imaging (see above, diameter of targeted area was approximately 850 µM around the center of the spot generated by intrinsic imaging).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of recorded neurons.

claim: Only recordings from neurons that showed firing properties characteristic of pyramidal neurons were included, whereas fast-spiking neurons were excluded.
source: Only recordings from neurons that showed firing properties characteristic of pyramidal neurons were included, whereas fast-spiking neurons were excluded.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.
